Only use approved icons.

The library currently only includes a subset of icons, and are for mock-up purposes only. If you need to create a mock-up with an icon that isn't available yet, just use a placeholder icon. Don't use unapproved icons in your work (for example, downloaded from Noun Project, or icons you've created yourself). If you have a question about icons, or would like to reach out to the Icons team directly, email icons@adobe.com or post in #icons on Slack.

Workflow icons are graphical metaphors or symbols that users interact with to navigate and manipulate objects. They maintain a consistent size and style within each platform to ensure visual harmony and usability. While consistency is key, it is now fairly common to combine different icon scales to support hierarchy and context. Image: Various examples of workflow icons, such as file folder, favorite, and layer. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_19d660d204b7c5e1a7c63b2222d9d074c750f5bd7.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

UI icons are atomic pieces — like arrows, crosses, or chevrons — that are part of a component. They aren't metaphorical per se, but they're an indication of how users interact with a component (for example, what happens when you click on a disclosure chevron or drag handle in a panel). Unlike workflow icons, UI icons come in assorted sizes. Image: Various examples of UI icons, including asterisks, hold affordances, and checkmarks. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_129452f026ebb116f3c0ab44ea5a9d0f39a46bf23.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

Badges (status and premium).

Status badges are indicators that communicate a variety of statuses or states, such as presence, validity, completeness, and more. Premium badges indicate that a feature is only available to paying customers. Image: Six cloud icons representing status badges: syncing, analytics, error, paused, warning, and connectivity, arranged in two rows. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1e67f94991d24dd8085a3be86ea3d8133fc229a25.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)Image: Icons and buttons showcasing premium features, including a crown, image badge, and gradient (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1201b1e81a17bd9420e0cff5d1d07db3605560c27.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

Cursors and HUD.

The cursor style has also been updated to match the look and feel of the Spectrum 2 icons. Image: A grid of 8 cursor icons on a gray background, including arrow, move, rotate, selection, eyedropper, pen tool, and hand pointer. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_16dbded183485739df532a9e5c6d8691ad98e088e.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)Image: Examples of HUD icons in an on-canvas experience, using an outlined style, such as a expand arrow set and a share action. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_18f38b43b49774ba7e2ee84bdf4f8d31f486346e8.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

Workflow icon sizes.

Spectrum 2 workflow icons come in two sizes per platform, but with one stroke weight: 1.5 px. The primary size for Desktop/Web is a canvas of 20 px with the icon being ~18 px. There's a secondary size for UI areas — like a layers panel, lists, or cards — which require smaller versions and come in a 16 px canvas with the icon being ~14 px. The equivalent for Mobile is the primary size of the canvas at 24 px with the icon being ~22 px. The secondary size canvas is 20 px with the icon being ~18px. Image: Desktop/Web UI sizing guide showing icon sizes (14px, 18px) and canvas sizes (16px, 20px) in 4px increments with labels. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1236e359414097f6bc99a83a12d01e1f93d08b158.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)Image: Mobile UI size guide showing icon sizes (18px, 22px) and canvas sizes (20px, 24px) with increments of 4px, labeled secondary and primary. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1515921a808568b3251961e02dd58984d15f85037.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

T-shirt sizes.

In Spectrum components, workflow icons scale up or down slightly when they're used. For example: a 20 px icon in a medium-sized component will be slightly larger in a large-sized component, and smaller in a small-sized component. UI icons come in their respective size range, since Spectrum components treat these differently.

S2" is the prefix for Spectrum 2 icons. Here's a breakdown of each part of the icon naming convention: Prefix identifies it as part of a larger group of assets. Type is the type of the asset: Icon, Ani-Icon, Ani-Illu, Illu, Cur, or Mock-Icon. Icon name is in Pascal case: there are no empty spaces or individual characters allowed. When names use multiple words, it utilizes a hierarchy to determine the word sequence. Icon canvas size is stated in pixel at @1x. Icon State indicator: normal state is "_N", selected state is "_S", and Dark UI theme adds a "D". Filetype suffix indicates the asset format, like SVG or PDF. Image: Key example of a naming convention for a Spectrum 2 icon, with parts differentiated by underscores in between. Prefix, S2. Type, Icon. Icon name in pascal case, TextAlignLeft. Size or hotspot, 20. State, N and UI theme, D. Period. File type suffix, SVG. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_173ea0c683d262b14b6650ec2b1e7c10bff15b4e9.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)An example of the naming convention for Spectrum 2 (S2) icons.

Stroke border (weight).

Keeping one stroke weight consistent within a size range helps to balance out and contrast the visual weight. For Web and Desktop platforms, icons are designed at a 20 px canvas as default with a 1.5 px stroke, resulting in a 1.64 px stroke when sized up to 24 px for mobile. This helps keep a unified look, and it builds icons efficiently since it's not necessary to redraw them for each platform. Image: Examples showing icon border width and in context of components. A Web or Desktop Edit icon has a size of 20 pixels and stroke width of 1.5 pixels, shown in selected and quiet variants of a button with icon, label Edit. A Mobile icon has a size of 24 pixels and a stroke width of 1.64 pixels, scaled, shown in selected and quiet variants of a button with icon, label Edit. The mobile buttons appear larger in size compared to the Web or Desktop buttons. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1217f999349e7af13d6bbbdd4a76179d6ba3cd1b7.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

Corner radius and shape rounding.

All icons with angles get a 1.5 px rounding treatment to achieve a rounder appearance. Inner corners are slightly rounded, and all stroke ends have rounded end caps. By default, the corner radius can be decreased in case a metaphor requires pointy edges. Image: Diagram showing an example of corner radius and shape rounding. A 20 pixel icon canvas shows an Add icon. The corner radius of the icon is 1.5 pixels, includes rounded end caps, and has a stroke weight of 1.5 pixels. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1d62ddcbe62292e82279c38806a2c28578aa7bee5.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

Icon and badges placement.

Icon designs include a safe area to ensure there's flexibility for finding the best positioning and balance in a layout. The main shape should be centered, and modifier placement is primarily at the bottom right corner of the canvas. Notification dots appear at the top right corner (these are mostly added programmatically). Image: Diagram showing how a badge and a modifier are placed together to create an Add People icon. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_164bc82f5960b835d1d59dacb5972fff363daf64b.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)The intersections of badge/modifier placement. Image: Diagram showing icon safe area. On Desktop, an icon has a 32 pixel canvas. 20 pixels are the icon, with a 4 pixel rounding area. Within the 20 pixels, there's an additional 1 pixel of space as a safe area. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_12be2561e5bfac5b291bc83f288f974a14693786a.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)Image: Diagram showing icon safe area. On Mobile, an icon has a 40 pixel canvas. 24 pixels are the icon, with a 5 pixel rounding area. Within the 24 pixels, there's an additional 1 pixel of space as a safe area. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1429c0c52bd33f83e03fb5948c936b12b806c7555.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

The vertical spacing between icons and text is adjusted to create balance. For example: in a medium-sized component, shifting the text box 1 px up and the icon box 1 px down inside a button better balances out the appearance and refines the relationship with text in Adobe Clean Medium. Image: Chart showing an example of how text and icons align. An icon is paired with a label, Overview. Total height, 32 pixels. Cap height, 11 pixels. Baseline, 12 pixels. Text box, 15 pixels. Icon frame, 20 pixels. Padding, between 6 and 9 pixels. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_183e169becf04f766797f939e070e2feca26723d5.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)An example of icon and text alignment in a button. Image: Chart showing the alignment of quiet action buttons to avatar, and a label in Adobe Clean typeface, regular, size 14. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_17303213bde9663c82bc06d81978fa55e70e1af66.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)An example of a quiet action button with a 16 px icon.

Advantages to the new SVG structure.

One SVG asset serves all states in all UI color themes Stable and easy creation and export workflows in Illustrator Streamlined SVG code for smaller file size Minimal effort to update any Spectrum color changes Allows for app-specific custom colors (a variable illustration accent color could be matched to the app color) Will become easier to add special colors for an app (for example, the brand red color used in Acrobat) Image: SVG code snippet with a clock icon and red exclamation mark, highlighting fill attributes for primary and red colors. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_15d13649c66a68f6bb49754c24ffe1e1222152cb3.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)Example of SVG code. The highlighted sections show that two dynamic colors will be changed programmatically, and that there's a white exclamation mark which should always be displayed in white.

documentBlocks.dont: All icons are crafted with a specific stroke weight, size, and canvas to match a larger icon set. Resizing or scaling them can change the appearance, creating inconsistency within a product. Ask for more sizes by submitting a request to the Icons team.

The Icons team works carefully to ensure that icon metaphors and style are consistent across Adobe products. When different product teams each decide to choose their own metaphors or build their own icons, this becomes a complex issue in Adobe's large product portfolio — and it shows our customers that we don't speak with a single brand voice. If you need a new icon for Spectrum 2, request it.

documentBlocks.content: Semantic colors have specific meanings in the design system. Choose icons with metaphors that visually align with their corresponding semantic color. Ensure that any semantic color usage in icons is consistent with Spectrum's usage. If you're using icons to convey "Success," "Alert," "Information," or "Caution" meanings (such as in an in-line alert ), use the appropriate colors. Image: Four status icons: green check, red warning triangle, blue info circle, orange caution diamond, each in colored square backgrounds. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1328a6f014c5f2f47807fcbf49242a379f61db1bc.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)Image: Four status icons: red checkmark, yellow warning triangle, green X, and gray exclamation mark, each in colored square backgrounds. (source: https://spectrum.adobe.com/foundations/icons-and-illustrations/media_1723d42953cb48ace9cec41dbdd127dde02bc5785.png?width=750&format=png&optimize=medium)

Meeting contrast requirements.

Using the available Spectrum 2 colors with Spectrum 2 icons will ensure that your design is both visually appealing and meets the WCAG minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 for non-text contrast. If you diverge from Spectrum colors, you'll need to make sure that your design has enough contrast between the icon and the background. Use subtle fills in light and dark themes to maintain legibility without overpowering the UI. Make sure that the icons remain legible and distinguishable across varied backgrounds and themes. The Stark plugin for Figma can help you check your contrast ratio. Consider three color combinations: A dark icon on a color background A light icon on a color background Tinted icons on a color background
